analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and restores the health care law as it stood before 2010.
analysis.headline: A Senate bill to repeal the Affordable Care Act, cosponsored by all 47 Senate Republicans, sat on the Senate calendar and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have wiped out the Affordable Care Act and the health care provisions of the 2010 reconciliation law, restoring the rules that existed before those laws passed. That would have ended the law's coverage expansions, its protections for people with pre-existing conditions, and its taxes on high earners and health industries.
analysis.who_benefits: Highest-income households and health industries: the law's 3.8% surtax on investment income and extra Medicare payroll tax on high earners, its tax on high-cost employer plans, its tax on medical devices, and its fees on insurers and drug makers would all disappear [S2] [S3]. Health insurers would shed the law's coverage rules, though they would also lose the mandate that brought them millions of new subsidized customers.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act as if it had never been enacted, effective back to the date of its enactment [S2] [S3].
Repeals the health care provisions of the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 and restores the prior law those provisions changed [S2] [S3].
Repeal would have removed the taxes the law imposed to finance its coverage expansion, including taxes falling on high earners, insurers, and medical device makers [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, ordinary people would have borne the cost: the law's coverage expansion, protections for people with pre-existing conditions, Medicaid expansion, subsidies, and other consumer protections would have ended with no replacement in the bill, returning health coverage to its pre-2010 rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: People covered by the ACA's protections

drawbacks.text: Repeal would have restored the pre-2010 legal landscape, in which insurers could deny or price out people with pre-existing conditions, impose lifetime benefit caps, and charge more for sick customers, ending those protections with nothing to replace them [S2] [S3].

The bill repealed the taxes that financed the law's coverage expansion without any replacement funding or replacement coverage program, so the tens of millions of people who had gained coverage through the law would have lost it [S2] [S3].

Supporters argued the law itself was a costly burden on employers, states, and individuals; this bill offered full repeal rather than a redesign, so even critics who wanted changes had no alternative proposal here.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For its supporters, repeal removed a law they considered an overreach that raised costs and mandated coverage. But the bill offered nothing in place of what it took away: the coverage expansions, pre-existing-condition protections, and subsidies would have ended while the tax cuts flowed mainly to high earners and health industries. As drafted, the costs to ordinary people clearly outweighed the benefits.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate's Democratic leadership never brought the bill up for a vote; it was placed on the Senate calendar a day after introduction and sat there until the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jim DeMint introduced the bill on January 26, 2011, with 40 original cosponsors, all Republicans [S3].
The bill had 47 cosponsors, all Republicans [S4].
The bill would have repealed the Affordable Care Act and the health provisions of the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, restoring prior law [S2] [S3].
It was read a second time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 4 on January 27, 2011 [S5] [S1].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee hearing or a floor vote before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People covered by the ACA's protections are better off that it died: the coverage expansions, pre-existing-condition rules, and subsidies stayed in place. High earners and health industries that would have gained from repeal of the law's taxes did not get that benefit.

for.name: Sen. Jim DeMint
for.role: U.S. Senator from South Carolina; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 26, 2011 and assembled the Senate's Republican cosponsors behind it

for.name: 47 of 47 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Every Senate Republican cosponsored the full repeal bill

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote after it was placed on the calendar

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Made clear he would veto any repeal of his signature health care law, removing any path to enactment even if the Senate had voted

sides.party_line_note: All 47 cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored it, while the Democratic Senate majority never scheduled a vote; the fight ran entirely along party lines.

industries.note: Repeal would have removed the law's rules on insurers and its fees on them, but it also would have ended the individual mandate and subsidies that made millions of people paying customers. Insurers gained from repeal's deregulation but lost its guaranteed market.
Repeal would have erased the law's 2.3% excise tax on medical devices, which helped finance the coverage expansion that device makers' customers relied on.
Repeal would have ended the law's drug industry fees and the Medicare coverage-gap discounts drug makers were required to give seniors, raising out-of-pocket drug costs for beneficiaries.
Repeal would have eliminated the law's additional Medicare taxes on high earners and its surtax on investment income, a direct tax cut concentrated at the top that was funding coverage for others.
